content: Have you ever seen trees swaying in a storm or felt the cool breeze on a hot summer day? Even though we cannot see air, it is everywhere around us. Ancient Indian texts like the Rigveda describe Vayu (Air) as the breath of the universe, a vital life force. Why can we feel it but never see it? Let's uncover the mystery of the invisible blanket around our Earth!
Think about this: If you take an 'empty' glass bottle and try to push it upside down into a bucket of water, why does the water not go inside easily? Is the bottle really empty?

content.title: The Empty Bottle Experiment
content.description: Watch as the upside-down bottle creates bubbles when tilted underwater. The air was occupying space inside the bottle!

content: The bottle wasn't empty at all; it was filled with **Air**! Air occupies space and is present everywhere around us. Our Earth is surrounded by a thin layer of air called the **Atmosphere**. Etymology: Atmosphere comes from Greek 'atmos' (vapour) and 'sphaira' (sphere).

content.definition: The thin blanket of air that surrounds the earth.

content.question: Why did the 'empty' bottle produce bubbles when tilted underwater?
options: Because air was escaping from the bottle

content: Reflection: Stand in front of a mirror and blow on it, or simply wave your hand in front of your face. Describe the sensation. Can you list three ways you can 'feel' air even though you can't see it?

Connection: Remember when we learned about how plants make food in earlier chapters? The air around us connects directly to Biology! Plants take in Carbon Dioxide from this invisible air to survive, and they give out Oxygen, which we breathe.

Mastery Challenge: Find a pinwheel (firki) or make one out of paper. Take it outside and try to find the direction in which the air is moving. Explain to a younger sibling how the invisible air is making the pinwheel spin!

Imagine a giant, invisible pizza floating in the sky. If you cut this 'air pizza' into slices, what would it be made of? Many centuries ago, people thought air was just one single substance. But today we know it's a mixture of many hidden ingredients!
If air is just one single gas, why do fires go out when we cover them with a glass, but they burn brightly in the open? Could there be a special gas in the air that helps things burn?

content.title: Composition of Air Pie Chart
content.description: A visual representation of the gases in the air. 78% Nitrogen, 21% Oxygen, and 1% other gases like Carbon Dioxide, Water Vapour, and dust.

content: Air is actually a mixture of many gases! The biggest slice (about 78%) is Nitrogen (Naitrojan), and the next big slice (about 21%) is Oxygen (Oksijan). The remaining 1% is Carbon Dioxide (Karban Dai-oksaid), water vapour, and dust. The Oxygen is the special gas that helps fires burn and keeps us alive!

content.definition: A gas present in air that is essential for breathing and burning.
The most abundant gas in the atmosphere, making up about 78% of the air.

content.question: Which gas makes up the largest part of the air around us?

content: Reflection: Close your eyes and take a deep breath. You just inhaled a mixture of gases. If our atmosphere was 100% Oxygen, what do you think would happen if someone lit a matchstick?

Connection: This connects to our Geography lessons about mountains! As you climb higher, the blanket of air becomes thinner. This is why mountaineers have to carry Oxygen cylinders with them to breathe!

Mastery Challenge: The Candle Experiment. Under adult supervision, light a small candle and carefully cover it with a transparent glass tumbler. Watch how it eventually goes out. Explain to your parents exactly which gas the candle 'used up'.

Have you ever wondered how fish survive underwater? Or how earthworms survive deep inside the mud? If animals need oxygen to breathe, where do they get it from when they are surrounded by water or soil? Let's dive deep into this mystery!

Think about a pot of water being heated on a stove. Long before the water starts boiling, you see tiny bubbles forming on the inner surface of the pot. Where do these bubbles come from? Can gases hide in liquids?

content.title: Bubbles in Heated Water
content.description: An animation showing dissolved air escaping as bubbles from water as it is heated.

content: The bubbles you see are the air dissolved in water! Aquatic animals use this dissolved Oxygen to breathe underwater. Similarly, air is trapped between the particles of soil, which allows plant roots and earthworms to breathe!
A common mistake is thinking that fish breathe the 'O' in H2O. They don't! They breathe the free Oxygen gas (O2) that is dissolved in the water, not the Oxygen atoms bonded in water molecules.

content.question: How do aquatic animals (like fish) breathe underwater?
options: They hold their breath for a long time
They use Oxygen dissolved in water
They come to the surface for every breath

content: Reflection: During heavy rains, earthworms come out of the soil. Why do you think they do that? Think about what happens to the spaces between the soil particles when it rains heavily.

Connection: The balance of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide in the atmosphere is maintained by plants and animals together. Plants release Oxygen during photosynthesis, and animals use it for respiration. A beautiful cycle of life!

Mastery Challenge: Take a lump of dry soil and put it in a glass of water. What do you observe? You will see bubbles coming out! Explain this phenomenon to your friends, proving that soil contains air.
